aiSummary: Choctawhatchee Bay is fishing well for speckled trout and redfish this Tuesday, with guides reporting consistent trout action bay-wide and bull reds in the mix — get on the water early before heat index values climb toward 103°F and the afternoon storm window opens after 1 PM. Today's new moon is driving spring tides, meaning stronger tidal pushes through creek mouths and oyster bars at both the early-morning high (5:07 AM) and the afternoon low (4:20 PM) — both transitions are worth targeting. Wind is light out of the west at 0–10 mph, water is 87°F and slightly stained, and a 12% storm chance after 1 PM is manageable if you plan to be off the water by early afternoon.

bridge.aiNote: The 331 Bridge spans the narrow neck of Choctawhatchee Bay, creating a current funnel where bait gets pushed through on both tides. Pilings hold speckled trout, redfish, sheepshead, and black drum year-round, with the lee-side pilings being the prime ambush zone on incoming tides. This is open, exposed water — it's typically the first spot to become unfishable when wind picks up and chop builds.
bridge.todaysCall: Light westerly wind at 0–10 mph means chop should be minimal at the bridge this morning, making it a fishable window before conditions can deteriorate. The new moon's spring tide already pushed through on the 5:07 AM high, so current should still be moving and concentrating bait around the pilings in the early hours — target the lee-side pilings as that flow relaxes. Bay-wide reports put trout active and widespread, so work the pilings with live shrimp or a soft plastic under a popping cork. Wrap up well before 1 PM given the afternoon storm window, and keep an eye on any wind increase that could quickly make this open-water spot uncomfortable.

alaqua.aiNote: Alaqua Bayou offers protected water with a strong year-round redfish population, plus speckled trout and flounder at the mouth. The oyster bars at the creek mouth are the prime structure to target, and tree cover keeps the bayou a few degrees cooler than the open bay while providing shelter from wind and weather. The upper creek transitions toward brackish water and can hold bass alongside smaller redfish.
alaqua.todaysCall: Alaqua is a smart pick today — the tree-lined banks offer shade and a break from the intense morning heat, and light westerly wind at 0–10 mph means the protected interior will be glassy. Work the oyster bars at the creek mouth during the morning hours while the new moon's spring tide is still in motion from the early high — stronger tidal flow here should push baitfish onto the bars and stack redfish and trout in the ambush zone. Bay-wide reports confirm redfish and trout are active, and this bayou's consistent red population makes it a reliable bet. Clear out before 1 PM to beat the afternoon storm window.

basin.aiNote: Basin Bayou sees less pressure than neighboring Alaqua and LaGrange, which tends to mean less-educated fish and a more relaxed fishing experience. The interior grass flats are classic sight-fishing territory for redfish in under two feet of water, and pompano occasionally show at the mouth on moving tides in late spring and early summer. It is somewhat less protected than LaGrange when weather builds.
basin.todaysCall: The new moon's spring tide will push stronger tidal flow through Basin Bayou's mouth this morning — arrive early to catch the tail end of that post-high movement and work the grass flat edges as bait gets swept in. Slightly stained water today means you can get closer to tailing or cruising reds on the interior flats without spooking them as easily, which is a small edge for sight fishing. Light westerly wind at 0–10 mph should be manageable here, though Basin offers less wind protection than LaGrange if a stray breeze builds. Plan to wrap up fishing by noon given the heat index and the 12% storm chance after 1 PM.

lagrange.aiNote: LaGrange Bayou is widely considered the top trout producer in this part of Choctawhatchee Bay, with legendary oyster bars at the mouth and interior grass flats that hold redfish year-round. Deep holes inside hold black drum and sheepshead, and the bayou offers the most protected water on this side of the bay. It is the go-to refuge when weather builds elsewhere.
lagrange.todaysCall: LaGrange is the strongest call on the board today — it's the bay's top trout producer, bay-wide reports confirm a steady and widespread trout bite, and the new moon's spring tide amplifies tidal flow over those legendary oyster-bar structures at the mouth. Fish the bars on the outgoing tide as it builds toward the 4:20 PM low, but given the heat and the afternoon storm window after 1 PM, focus your prime effort on the early morning hours instead. Slightly stained water and bright sun make the interior grass flats trickier for sight fishing midday, so prioritize the oyster structure and deeper interior holes early. This is also the safest spot to stay longer if conditions deteriorate, since it's the most protected water in the area.

fourmile.aiNote: Four Mile Creek is a tidal creek running between Shipyard Marina and the bay, where tidal flow pushes baitfish up the creek on incoming tides and concentrates redfish and trout in the bends and along grass edges. The creek mouth is a prime flounder zone, and the upper section transitions toward brackish water that can hold bass alongside smaller reds. Short and well-protected, it is consistently the safest fishery when weather is a concern.
fourmile.todaysCall: Four Mile Creek is an excellent early-morning option today — it's short, protected, and the new moon's spring tide will have been pushing baitfish into the bends since before first light. Work the bends and grass edges in the lower and middle sections during the morning as that tidal flow continues to relax after the 5:07 AM high. The creek mouth is worth a few casts for flounder, especially in the slightly stained water where they tend to ambush readily. If afternoon storms threaten, this is your safest bailout spot — you can fish right up to the storm window without worrying much about exposure.

hogtown.aiNote: Hogtown Bayou is a signature Santa Rosa Beach guide destination and one of the most consistently productive trout flats on Choctawhatchee Bay. Summer mornings are peak time, with trout stacked on grass in two to four feet of water, and Spanish mackerel show at the mouth on moving tides. It sees regular guide pressure but produces reliably, though it is farther from the 331 Bridge than the other bayous — factor in run time.
hogtown.todaysCall: Hogtown is arguably the top trout flat call today — bay-wide reports specifically name Santa Rosa Beach guides finding good trout numbers, and this is their signature spot. Get there early: summer mornings are when trout are stacked on the grass in two to four feet, and the new moon's spring tide adds extra tidal movement to fire up the bite. The longer run from the 331 area means you want to be idling into position before or right at sunrise (6:07 AM), so plan your departure accordingly. Check the bayou mouth for Spanish mackerel on any tidal movement, and be wheels-up well before 1 PM to beat both the heat and the afternoon storm window on the longer run home.

mallet.aiNote: Mallet Bayou is a small tributary that feeds directly into LaGrange Bayou just south of Freeport. Its direct connection to LaGrange — this dashboard's top trout producer — means LaGrange's oyster-bar trout-and-redfish pattern plausibly extends into this quieter, smaller water, though documented fishing history for Mallet Bayou itself is limited. Its small, interior character makes it a likely calm-water fallback when wind picks up on the open bay.
mallet.todaysCall: Mallet is worth considering today as a quieter extension of the LaGrange complex — if the main bayou mouth is seeing pressure, slip into Mallet for a less-pressured look at what should be a similar trout-and-redfish pattern. The new moon's spring tide will push water through the connection between Mallet and LaGrange, so fish any current seams or structure near that junction early in the morning. Light westerly wind at 0–10 mph means wind is not a driver today, but Mallet's small, interior nature keeps it calm regardless. Treat it as a complement to a LaGrange trip rather than a standalone destination, and keep the 1 PM storm window in mind.

mack.aiNote: Mack Bayou sits on the barrier-island, 30-A side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park — a long run from the 331 Bridge and not a quick local trip. It shares the protected-bayou character of Alaqua and LaGrange, with marsh grass, oyster bars, and a few interior holes, and sees lighter pressure simply due to its distance. Hewett Bayou and Buck Bayou sit immediately to the east and are realistically fishable in the same trip.
mack.todaysCall: If you are willing to make the long run, Mack Bayou offers light pressure and the same oyster-bar and marsh-grass habitat that is producing redfish and trout bay-wide right now. The new moon's spring tide means stronger flow at the mouth — time your arrival to fish the outgoing tide building toward the afternoon low, but with a long run home and a storm window after 1 PM, commit to an early departure. Slightly stained water should keep fish less wary along the oyster structure. Pair Mack with Hewett on the same trip to make the run worthwhile, and have a firm turnaround time to beat afternoon weather.

hewett.aiNote: Hewett Bayou sits immediately east of Mack Bayou on the barrier-island, 30-A side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park — another long-run destination that pairs naturally with Mack and Buck Bayou in a single trip. It offers the same protected habitat as its neighbors, including oyster bars and marsh grass at the mouth and a few deeper interior holes farther in. Light fishing pressure is a consistent advantage here thanks to the distance from main boat ramps.
hewett.todaysCall: Hewett benefits from the same light-pressure, protected-bayou formula as Mack next door, and today's bay-wide trout-and-redfish bite gives you reason to make the run. Fish the oyster bars at the mouth during the morning tidal movement driven by the new moon's spring tide, then explore the interior holes for any stacked fish before heat shuts things down. The long run home under a 103°F heat index and a post-1 PM storm window means you need a firm turnaround — plan to be heading back by noon at the latest. Pair with Mack and optionally Buck to make the distance count.

buck.aiNote: Buck Bayou is the smallest and least-documented of the three neighboring bayous on the barrier-island, 30-A side of Choctawhatchee Bay near Topsail Hill Preserve State Park. Its habitat should mirror its larger neighbors — marsh grass, some oyster structure, and a modest interior — but there is less basis to speak with confidence about it. It is best treated as a bonus stop on a Mack and Hewett Bayou trip rather than a standalone destination worth a long run on its own.
buck.todaysCall: Buck is a reasonable bonus cast on a Mack-and-Hewett trip today — poke in, work any visible oyster structure at the mouth during tidal movement from the new moon's spring tide, and move on if it doesn't produce quickly. With limited documented history here, don't burn significant time that could be better spent at Mack or Hewett where the habitat is better understood. Slightly stained water and light westerly wind keep conditions manageable on this side of the bay. As with the other long-run 30-A spots, have a firm noon turnaround in mind to beat the heat and the afternoon storm window on the run back.
